authors: Canadian Cancer Registries Epidemiology Research Group
validated_results.journal: European journal of cancer prevention : the official journal of the European Cancer Prevention Organisation (ECP)
validated_results.reason: Population-based case-control study of processed meat intake assessed by FFQ with incident histologically confirmed bladder cancer as an outcome; a bladder-specific odds ratio value is not itemized in the abstract but the target context is reported.

extraction.comparison_type: Highest versus lowest quartile of processed meat intake
extraction.timing: retrospective (eating habits 2 years before the study, 1994-1997)
extraction.population: Patients with histologically confirmed incident cancer and population controls

sample_size.excerpt: Mailed questionnaires were completed by 19 732 patients with histologically confirmed incident cancer of the stomach, colon, rectum, pancreas, lung, breast, ovary, prostate, testis, kidney, bladder, brain, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma or leukaemia, and 5039 population controls,between 1994 and 1997. Measurement included information on socioeconomic status, lifestyle habits and diet.
sample_size.location: abstract, methods; total_n derived from reported group counts 19732 + 5039 = 24771

effect_size.excerpt: Processed meat was significantly related to the risk of the stomach, colon, rectum, pancreas, lung, prostate, testis, kidney and bladder cancer and leukaemia

comparison.excerpt: the odds ratios for the highest quartile ranged from 1.3 to 1.7

design.excerpt: Odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals were derived through unconditional logistic regression.

timing.excerpt: A 69-item food frequency questionnaire provided data on eating habits 2 years before the study.

exposure_measurement.excerpt: A 69-item food frequency questionnaire provided data on eating habits

gender.excerpt: incident cancer of the stomach, colon, rectum, pancreas, lung, breast, ovary, prostate, testis, kidney, bladder

extraction.ethnicity_basis: NA: no field-specific ethnicity evidence was available

parallel_r3_gate_reasons: important quantitative evidence remains missing or invalid: cases, ci_lower, ci_upper, effect_size, p_value

validated_results.title: Dietary intake of micronutrients and the risk of developing bladder cancer: results from the Belgian case-control study on bladder cancer risk.
validated_results.reason: Case-control study reporting a dietary calcium intake odds ratio for incident bladder cancer.

extraction.comparison_type: Highest versus lowest category of dietary calcium intake
extraction.timing: retrospective dietary assessment by food frequency questionnaire
extraction.population: Participants in the Belgian case-control study on bladder cancer risk

sample_size.excerpt: A semi-quantitative 322 item food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) was used to collect dietary data from 200 bladder cancer cases and 386 control subjects participating in the Belgian case-control study on bladder cancer risk.
sample_size.location: abstract, methods; total_n derived from reported group counts 200 + 386 = 586

cases.excerpt: A semi-quantitative 322 item food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) was used to collect dietary data from 200 bladder cancer cases and 386 control subjects participating in the Belgian case-control study on bladder cancer risk.

effect_size.excerpt: We observed a positive association between calcium intake and bladder cancer (OR: 1.77; 95% CI: 1.00-3.15; p-trend = 0.049) and increased odds, although not statistically significant, for highest tertile of phosphorus intake (OR: 1.82; 95% CI: 0.95-3.49; p-trend = 0.06).

confidence_interval.excerpt: We observed a positive association between calcium intake and bladder cancer (OR: 1.77; 95% CI: 1.00-3.15; p-trend = 0.049) and increased odds, although not statistically significant, for highest tertile of phosphorus intake (OR: 1.82; 95% CI: 0.95-3.49; p-trend = 0.06).

validated_results.title: Red meat, dietary nitrosamines, and heme iron and risk of bladder cancer in the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC).
validated_results.journal: Cancer epidemiology, biomarkers & prevention : a publication of the American Association for Cancer Research, cosponsored by the American Society of Preventive Oncology
validated_results.reason: Prospective EPIC cohort reporting a hazard ratio for dietary heme iron intake and incident bladder cancer.

extraction.comparison_type: log2 (per doubling) increase in heme iron intake
extraction.population: Participants of the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC)

sample_size.excerpt: Data on food consumption and complete follow-up for cancer occurrence were available for a total of 481,419 participants, recruited in 10 European countries.

cases.excerpt: After a mean follow-up of 8.7 years, 1,001 participants were diagnosed with bladder cancer.

effect_size.excerpt: We found no overall association between intake of red meat (log2 HR: 1.06; 95% CI: 0.99-1.13), nitrosamines (log2 HR: 1.09; 95% CI: 0.92-1.30 and HR: 0.98; 95% CI: 0.92-1.05 for ENOC and NDMA, respectively) or heme iron (log2 HR: 1.05; 95 CI: 0.99-1.12) and bladder cancer risk.

confidence_interval.excerpt: We found no overall association between intake of red meat (log2 HR: 1.06; 95% CI: 0.99-1.13), nitrosamines (log2 HR: 1.09; 95% CI: 0.92-1.30 and HR: 0.98; 95% CI: 0.92-1.05 for ENOC and NDMA, respectively) or heme iron (log2 HR: 1.05; 95 CI: 0.99-1.12) and bladder cancer risk.
